components.note: 小 (small) — three small dots, tiny grains. As a radical it appears in 少 few, 尖 sharp.
日 (sun) — day and time, as in 晴 clear, 早 early, 明 bright; time was read from the sun.
寸 (cùn) stands in for 寺 sì in the traditional 時; sound clue is loose. 寺 also gives 诗 shī and 持 chí.

example.hanzi: 这趟火车要开三个小时。
example.pinyin: Zhè tàng huǒchē yào kāi sān gè xiǎoshí.
example.english: This train ride takes three hours.
example.fact: 小时 literally means “small hour” — 时 alone already meant a broader unit of time (as in 时候, also in this deck's pilot batch), and prefixing 小 narrowed it down specifically to the 24th-of-a-day measure borrowed from the Western clock, distinct from 时辰, the older 2-hour unit traditional Chinese timekeeping used.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ měitiān shuì bā ge xiǎoshí.
examples.english: I sleep eight hours every day.

examples.pinyin: Děng wǒ yí ge xiǎoshí, hǎo ma?
examples.english: Wait for me for an hour, okay?

components.note: 重 (zhòng) is a sound clue for 种 zhǒng/zhòng; it means heavy (zhòng) or to repeat (chóng, as in 重新).
要 (want, need) — oldest form shows hands at a waist: it meant "waist" (腰 yāo adds 月 flesh); "essential" followed.

example.english: Health is more important than anything.
example.fact: 重 is a heteronym: read zhòng it means “heavy” or “important” (as here), but read chóng the same character means “to repeat, again” (as in 重复) — two unrelated jobs split across one character by pronunciation alone.

examples.pinyin: Xué hǎo Zhōngwén duì wǒ hěn zhòngyào.
examples.english: Learning Chinese well is very important to me.

examples.pinyin: Zhè shì yí ge zhòngyào de huìyì.
examples.english: This is an important meeting.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — words and language, as in 说, 请, 话.
炎 (yán) is a close sound clue for tán; 炎 also sounds out 淡 dàn and 痰 tán.

example.english: Let's have a talk.
example.fact: 谈 is a more serious 'talk' than 说: 谈工作 'discuss work', 谈判 'negotiate'. 谈恋爱 means 'to date, be in a romantic relationship'. 谈话 'a talk' can be a formal conversation.

examples.pinyin: Wǒmen tántan jīntiān de jìhuà.
examples.english: Let's talk about today's plan.

examples.pinyin: Tāmen zài tán gōngzuò de shìqing.
examples.english: They are discussing work matters.

components.note: 刂 (knife) — cutting, as in 到, 分, 刻; to cut apart means separate.
另 (lìng, other) — separating things into "other" parts: 别 is another, different, or "don't".
人 (person) — a side-view figure of a person walking. As a radical it appears as 亻 on the left: 你 他 们.

example.pinyin: Bú yào zǒngshì hé biéren bǐjiào.
example.english: Don't always compare yourself to other people.
example.fact: 别 carries two unrelated jobs that both show up in this deck: as 别人's “other, separate” (from cutting things apart with a 刂 knife), and — completely independently — as a bare command meaning “don't” (别说, “don't say it”), a shortening of 不要 that has nothing to do with “separateness” at all.

examples.hanzi: 别人都走了,只有我留下。
examples.pinyin: Biérén dōu zǒu le, zhǐyǒu wǒ liúxià.
examples.english: Everyone else left; only I stayed.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ bú yào zǒngshì wèn biérén.
examples.english: Don't always ask other people.

components.note: 田 (field) — a field above 力 (strength): a man is one who works the fields with strength.
人 (person) — a side-view figure of a person walking. As a radical it appears as 亻 on the left: 你 他 们.

example.english: That man is fixing a bicycle.
example.fact: 男 is one of Mandarin's more transparent compositional characters: 田 (“field”) stacked over 力 (“strength, muscular effort”) pictures exactly the ancient division of labor the word encodes — a man was, by this character's logic, defined as the one strong enough to work the fields.

examples.pinyin: Zhège nánrén shì wǒ de línjū.
examples.english: This man is my neighbor.

examples.hanzi: 男人和女人都可以参加。
examples.pinyin: Nánrén hé nǚrén dōu kěyǐ cānjiā.
examples.english: Both men and women can take part.

components.note: 页 (head, page) — in traditional 頭 (豆 + 页): 页 is an old picture of a head, as in 顶, 领, 额. 头 dropped both parts.
大 (big) — the bottom. Memory aid: a big 大 body with two dots ⺀ like eyes above — the head, as in 头发. The dictionary's reading is loose.

example.english: My head hurts a lot.
example.fact: 头 is 'head' and the suffix of nouns: 石头 'stone', 木头 'wood', 骨头 'bone'. It also means 'first/top': 头一次 'the first time'. 头发 is 'hair', and 一头牛 counts a head of cattle.

examples.pinyin: Tā de tóufa hěn duǎn.
examples.english: His hair is very short.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ cóng tóu dào wěi dōu méi shuōhuà.
examples.english: I didn't say a word from start to finish.

components.note: 木 (tree) — wood, as in 树, 林, 桌; the older meaning was a wooden mechanism.
几 (jī) gives the exact sound; also in 饥 jī and 肌 jī.
会 (meet, can) — simplified from 會, a lid on a container: bringing things together; hence meeting, then "can" (huì).

example.pinyin: Zhè shì yí gè hěn hǎo de jīhuì.
example.english: This is a very good opportunity.
example.fact: 机 originally meant a mechanical device or trigger mechanism (from 木 “wood” plus 几, an old stool or table shape suggesting a wooden contraption) — 机会 pairs that “trigger” sense with 会 (“a meeting, a coming-together”) into something like “the moment the mechanism clicks into place,” a vivid image behind the everyday word for “opportunity.”

examples.pinyin: Wǒ méiyǒu jīhuì qù Zhōngguó.
examples.english: I don't have a chance to go to China.

examples.pinyin: Bié cuòguò zhège jīhuì.
examples.english: Don't miss this opportunity.

components.note: 山 (mountain) — the top part and radical, as in 岛 island. 岁 is simplified from 歲; Memory aid: a mountain of evenings (夕) passing makes years, 万岁 'long live'.
夕 (evening) — the bottom part, as in 外 and 多. It stands for passing time, so a year is many evenings; memory aid.

example.english: My daughter is five years old.
example.fact: 岁 gives age: 三岁 'three years old'. Ask a child 你几岁了？ and an adult 你多大了？ Respectfully, an elder is asked 您多大年纪？ The word also appears in 岁月 'years, time'.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ jīnnián duōshao suì?
examples.english: How old are you this year?

examples.hanzi: 他才三岁，已经会唱歌了。
examples.pinyin: Tā cái sān suì, yǐjīng huì chànggē le.
examples.english: He's only three and can already sing.

components.note: 凵 (open pit) — oldest form shows a foot stepping out of a pit or cave: to go out, come out.
土 (earth) — the top part, the ground family as in 地, 场, 块. Memory aid: leave the ground 土 and go off on your own 厶 path.
厶 (private, small loop) — the bottom part. Old forms show a person leaving a place, so the 土 story is only a mnemonic.

example.hanzi: 外面在下雨,你还要出去吗?
example.pinyin: Wàimiàn zài xiàyǔ, nǐ hái yào chūqù ma?
example.english: It's raining outside, do you still want to go out?
example.fact: 出去 combines two directional verbs — 出 (“to exit, emerge”) and 去 (“to go,” moving away from the speaker) — into a single compound that, like 出来 and 进去, packs both the direction of motion and its relation to the speaker's position into one word, a category English usually splits across separate prepositions.

examples.pinyin: Wǎnshang wǒ hěn shǎo chūqù.
examples.english: I rarely go out in the evening.

examples.pinyin: Tā názhe bāo chūqù le.
examples.english: He went out carrying a bag.

components.note: 氵 (water) — water and liquids, as in 河, 海, 汤; water means life: 活 is alive.
舌 (shé, tongue) is a loose sound clue for huó; also in 话 huà.

example.pinyin: Zhè tiáo yú hái huó zhe.
example.english: This fish is still alive.
example.fact: 活 is 'alive' and 'to live': 生活 'life', 活动 'activity', 活泼 'lively'. In speech 活 can also mean 'work': 干活 'do work'. It is different from 住 'live in (a place)'.

examples.pinyin: Zhè zhī niǎo hái huózhe.
examples.english: This bird is still alive.

examples.hanzi: 他们在大城市生活了很多年。
examples.pinyin: Tāmen zài dà chéngshì shēnghuóle hěn duō nián.
examples.english: They lived in a big city for many years.

components.note: 手 (hand) — over 目 (eye): a hand shading the eyes to look into the distance. 目 marks seeing words, as in 眼, 睡.
见 (see) — a big eye on a person's legs 儿: a person looking. The same 见 is in 现 appear, 觉 sense, 视 look.

example.hanzi: 我在路上看见了你的朋友。
example.pinyin: Wǒ zài lùshang kànjiàn le nǐ de péngyou.
example.english: I saw your friend on the road.
example.fact: 看 alone means the deliberate act of looking, but doesn't guarantee anything registered — attaching 见 (“to perceive”) as a result complement turns it into 看见, “to look and successfully perceive,” the same success-complement pattern behind 听见 (“to hear,” listen + perceive) and 找到 (“to find,” search + arrive-at-a-result).

examples.pinyin: Wǒ méi kànjiàn nǐ de yàoshi.
examples.english: I didn't see your keys.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ kànjiàn wǒ de yǎnjìng le ma?
examples.english: Have you seen my glasses?

components.note: 者 (zhě) is a sound clue for 都 dū, 著 zhù, 煮 zhǔ, 猪 zhū and 诸 zhū; as a word it means "one who", as in 作者 author.

example.english: He is an author.
example.fact: 者 is a suffix for people: 作者 'author', 记者 'journalist', 读者 'reader', 学者 'scholar'. In classical Chinese it means 'the one who…'. It never stands alone in modern speech.

examples.pinyin: Zhè wèi jìzhě hěn niánqīng.
examples.english: This reporter is very young.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ shì yí ge àihàozhě.
examples.english: I am an enthusiast.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — hand actions, as in 拿, 抱, 把; 打 is to hit.
丁 (dīng) is a loose sound clue for dǎ; 丁 also sounds out 订 dìng, 顶 dǐng and 钉 dīng.
电 (electric) — simplified from 電: 雨 rain over 申, a lightning bolt (申 originally pictured a flash).
讠 (speech) — words and language, as in 说, 请, 谢; 话 is speech.
舌 (shé, tongue) fits the meaning (speaking) and is a loose sound clue for huà; also in 活 huó.

example.pinyin: Wǒ míngtiān gěi nǐ dǎ diànhuà.
example.english: I'll call you tomorrow.
example.fact: 打 is one of Mandarin's most overloaded verbs of “impact, action” — literally “to hit,” it extends metaphorically into dozens of set collocations with nothing to do with striking, including 打电话 (“make a call”), 打的 (“hail a taxi”), and 打扫 (“to clean”), each pairing 打 with a different object to produce an unrelated action.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ wǎnshang gěi wǒ dǎ diànhuà ba.
examples.english: Give me a call tonight.

examples.hanzi: 他正在打电话,请等一下。
examples.pinyin: Tā zhèngzài dǎ diànhuà, qǐng děng yíxià.
examples.english: He's on the phone; please wait a moment.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — marks speech, sounds and eating, as in 叫 call, 吃 eat, 唱 sing; 喂 is a hello on the phone or a call for attention; also to feed.
畏 (wèi) — same sound: 喂 wèi. 畏 also sounds out 煨 wēi.

example.pinyin: Wèi, qǐngwèn shì Wáng xiānsheng ma?
example.english: Hello, may I ask if this is Mr. Wang?
example.fact: 喂 is the standard phone 'hello', also read wéi by some speakers. It is also a verb, 'to feed': 喂孩子 'feed the child', 喂狗 'feed the dog'. Use it to call someone's attention, but it can sound blunt.

examples.pinyin: Wèi, wǒ shì Xiǎo Wáng, nǐ zài nǎr?
examples.english: Hello, this is Xiao Wang, where are you?

examples.pinyin: Māma zài wèi xiǎohái chīfàn.
examples.english: Mom is feeding the child.

components.note: 女 (woman) — women and family, as in 妈, 她, 姐.
子 (child) — a woman with her child: the picture of something good.
亻 (person) — people, as in 你, 他, 做; 像 is a person's likeness.
象 (xiàng, elephant) gives the exact sound; 象 first meant elephant, then "image".

example.english: He doesn't seem too happy.
example.fact: 好像 softens a claim into a guess or impression (“it seems as if...”) and, unlike English “seem,” can open a sentence on its own with no dummy subject needed — 好像要下雨了 (“it looks like it's going to rain”) has no equivalent of English's placeholder “it.”

examples.pinyin: Zhège háizi hǎoxiàng tā bàba.
examples.english: This child looks like his father.

examples.pinyin: Tiān hǎoxiàng yào xiàyǔ le.
examples.english: It looks like it's going to rain.

components.note: 彳 (step) — walking and going, as in 行, 往, 很 very.
寸 (hand) — oldest form is a hand grabbing a cowrie shell (money): 得 is "to obtain". The shell has worn down to 旦.
至 (arrive) — 到 is to arrive.
刂 is the knife form 刀 (dāo), a close sound clue for dào; 到 itself sounds out 倒 dǎo/dào.

example.hanzi: 他的努力终于得到了回报。
example.pinyin: Tā de nǔlì zhōngyú dédào le huíbào.
example.english: His hard work finally got rewarded.
example.fact: 得到 pairs 得 (“to obtain” — a hand reaching for a valuable shell, per its own etymology) with 到 (“to arrive, to reach”) into “obtaining by reaching” — while its plain root 得 alone can also act as a purely grammatical particle in other contexts (记得, 觉得, both elsewhere in this deck) with no “obtaining” sense left at all.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ xiǎng dédào yí fèn hǎo gōngzuò.
examples.english: I want to get a good job.

examples.pinyin: Tā dédàole lǎoshī de biǎoyáng.
examples.english: She received praise from her teacher.

components.note: 言 (speech) — written 讠 on the left of other characters: a warning is spoken.
敬 (jìng, respect) is a close sound clue for jǐng.
宀 (roof) — houses and shelter, as in 家, 安, 室: to look carefully inside.
祭 (jì) is a loose sound clue for chá; 祭 also sounds out 际 jì and 擦 cā.

example.hanzi: 警察正在调查这起案件。
example.pinyin: Jǐngchá zhèngzài diàochá zhè qǐ ànjiàn.
example.english: The police are investigating this case.
example.fact: 警 and 察 are near-synonyms doubled together — 警 carries “to warn, to alert” (built from 言, speech) and 察 carries “to observe closely, to inspect” (built from 宀, a roof, evoking careful indoor scrutiny) — combining “alertness” with “close observation” into the job description behind “police.”

examples.pinyin: Jǐngchá zài lùkǒu zhǐhuī jiāotōng.
examples.english: The police officer is directing traffic at the intersection.

examples.hanzi: 如果你迷路了,可以问警察。
examples.pinyin: Rúguǒ nǐ mílù le, kěyǐ wèn jǐngchá.
examples.english: If you get lost, you can ask a police officer.

components.note: 宀 (roof) — houses and shelter, as in 家, 安, 室; 完 first meant complete, whole.
元 (yuán) is a close sound clue for wán; 元 also sounds out 玩 wán, 院 yuàn and 远 yuǎn.

example.english: I've finished my homework.
example.fact: 完 is a common result ending: 吃完 'finish eating', 写完, 看完. Alone, 完了 means 'it's over' or 'oh no!'. 完全 means 'completely'.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ chīwán le ma?
examples.english: Have you finished eating?

examples.pinyin: Zhè běn shū wǒ hái méi kànwán.
examples.english: I haven't finished reading this book yet.

components.note: 弓 (bow) — bows and stretching, as in 弯 bend, 弹 pluck, 引 draw: 张 is to draw a bow.
长 (zhǎng) is a close sound clue for zhāng.

example.pinyin: Wǒ mǎi le liǎng zhāng piào.
example.english: I bought two tickets.
example.fact: 张 counts flat things: 纸 'paper', 票 'tickets', 桌子 'tables', 床 'beds', 照片 'photos'. It is also the very common surname Zhāng, and 张开 means 'to open wide'.

examples.pinyin: Qǐng gěi wǒ yì zhāng báizhǐ.
examples.english: Please give me a sheet of white paper.

examples.hanzi: 你的桌子上有一张照片。
examples.pinyin: Nǐ de zhuōzi shang yǒu yì zhāng zhàopiàn.
examples.english: There is a photo on your desk.

components.note: 儿 (child, legs) — shows a person's legs; in 兒 the top was a child's soft skull. As an ending (这儿) it adds the er sound; 儿 also in 先, 兄, 光.
子 (child) — a picture of a baby with arms outstretched and legs bundled. As a suffix (孩子, 房子) it is a light noun ending.

example.hanzi: 他们的儿子已经上大学了。
example.pinyin: Tāmen de érzi yǐjīng shàng dàxué le.
example.english: Their son is already in college.
example.fact: 儿 on its own is a pictograph of a small child (a big head over a small body) and separately doubles as Mandarin's diminutive r-suffix (儿化, as in 这儿, “here”) — 儿子 keeps 儿's original “child” meaning intact, distinguishing it from that purely phonetic suffix use.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ érzi jīnnián bā suì.
examples.english: My son is eight this year.

examples.hanzi: 他有两个儿子和一个女儿。
examples.pinyin: Tā yǒu liǎng ge érzi hé yí ge nǚ'ér.
examples.english: He has two sons and a daughter.

meanings: (at the beginning of a sentence) afterwards

components.note: 之 (of, go) — oldest form is a foot leaving a starting line: "to go". Now it is a literary particle meaning "of" or "it".
后 (after, behind) — two words merged in simplified writing: old 后 "ruler" (皇后 empress) and 後 "behind, later" (as in 然后).

example.hanzi: 下课之后,我们去打篮球。
example.pinyin: Xiàkè zhīhòu, wǒmen qù dǎ lánqiú.
example.english: After class, let's go play basketball.
example.fact: 之后 mirrors 之前 (rank 104, also in this batch) as its exact opposite — both attach after the event they're relative to (X之后/之前) rather than before it the way English “after X” / “before X” do, so the two form a matched pair of time-relation markers built the same way.

examples.pinyin: Chīwán fàn zhīhòu, wǒ qù sànbù.
examples.english: After finishing dinner, I go for a walk.

examples.pinyin: Sān tiān zhīhòu, tā jiù huíguó le.
examples.english: Three days later, he went back to his country.

components.note: 氵 (water) — water, as in 河, 海, 汤; 漂 is to float.
票 (piào) gives the exact sound; also in 飘 piāo.
亮 (liàng) is a sound clue for 谅 liàng and 晾 liàng; as a word it means bright, as in 月亮 moon.

example.hanzi: 她今天穿的裙子很漂亮。
example.pinyin: Tā jīntiān chuān de qúnzi hěn piàoliang.
example.english: The skirt she's wearing today is very pretty.
example.fact: 漂 carries multiple readings depending on the word: piāo means “to float, drift” (its most common reading, as in 漂浮), piǎo means “to bleach” (漂白), and piào is reserved specifically for 漂亮 — a reminder that a whole word's pronunciation can diverge from a character's default reading, tripping up learners who default to piāoliang.

examples.pinyin: Zhè duǒ huā zhēn piàoliang.
examples.english: This flower is really pretty.

examples.hanzi: 你把房间打扫得很漂亮。
examples.pinyin: Nǐ bǎ fángjiān dǎsǎo de hěn piàoliang.
examples.english: You cleaned the room beautifully.

components.note: 刀 (knife) — cutting, as in 切, 刻, 到: a blade splits.
八 (eight) — originally two lines pulling apart: divide. 分 also gives 份 fèn, 粉 fěn and 纷 fēn.
钅 (metal, simplified 金) — metals, as in 钱, 铁, 错: a bell is cast metal.
中 (zhōng) gives the exact sound; 中 also means middle.

example.hanzi: 电影再过十分钟就开始了。
example.pinyin: Diànyǐng zài guò shí fēnzhōng jiù kāishǐ le.
example.english: The movie starts in ten more minutes.
example.fact: 钟 literally means “bell” or, by extension, “clock” (bells and later clocks were traditionally made of metal, hence the 钅 radical) — 分钟 literally reads as “a divided portion (分) of the clock (钟),” a compositional logic that mirrors English “minute” coming from Latin “minutus,” a “small” division of the hour.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ děngle nǐ èrshí fēnzhōng.
examples.english: I waited for you for twenty minutes.

examples.hanzi: 走路到学校只要五分钟。
examples.pinyin: Zǒulù dào xuéxiào zhǐ yào wǔ fēnzhōng.
examples.english: It only takes five minutes to walk to school.

components.note: 扌 (hand) — hand actions, as in 打, 拿, 抱: receiving something by hand.
妾 (qiè) is only a loose sound clue for jiē.

example.english: I'll go to the airport to pick you up.
example.fact: 接 means 'pick up' (a person), 'answer' (接电话) and 'connect'. 接受 means 'accept' and 接着 'then, next'. Its opposite for people is 送 'see off'.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ néng lái chēzhàn jiē wǒ ma?
examples.english: Can you pick me up at the station?

examples.pinyin: Māma jiēle yí ge diànhuà.
examples.english: Mom took a phone call.

components.note: 土 (earth) — ground and place, as in 地, 城, 坐: a field or open space.
昜 (yáng) is the traditional sound part, a loose clue for chǎng; the same part is in 汤 tāng, 扬 yáng and 肠 cháng.

example.pinyin: Zuótiān xià le yì chǎng dà yǔ.
example.english: There was a heavy rain yesterday.
example.fact: 场 counts events: 一场电影, 一场比赛, 一场大雨. It also names places: 机场 'airport', 市场 'market', 广场 'square'. Read cháng, it means 'threshing floor'.

examples.pinyin: Jīnwǎn yǒu yì chǎng zúqiú bǐsài.
examples.english: There is a soccer match tonight.

examples.pinyin: Wǒmen zài shìchǎng mǎi shuǐguǒ.
examples.english: We buy fruit at the market.

components.note: 冉 (rǎn) — the main part. The dictionary story is two fish on a line 一: a second catch, so 'again'. It is a memory aid; the origin is unclear.
一 (one) — the top bar. Memory aid: 'one more' line on top — 再见 see you again, 再次 once more.
见 (see) — a big eye on a person's legs 儿: a person looking. The same 见 is in 现 appear, 觉 sense, 视 look.

example.english: Okay, goodbye!
example.fact: 再见 is literally “see (you) again” — 再 (“once more, again”) plus 见 (“to see”) — making it structurally closer to French “au revoir” or Spanish “hasta la vista” than to English “goodbye,” which instead comes from a contraction of “God be with ye.”

examples.pinyin: Míngtiān jiàn, zàijiàn!
examples.english: See you tomorrow, bye!

examples.pinyin: Tā huīhui shǒu, shuōle shēng zàijiàn.
examples.english: He waved and said goodbye.

components.note: 求 (seek) — the original picture of a fur coat (裘 qiú adds 衣); "seek, request" is a borrowed use. 求 sounds out 球 qiú and 救 jiù.

example.pinyin: Wǒ qiú nǐ bāng wǒ yí ge máng.
example.english: I beg you to do me a favour.
example.fact: 求 is stronger than 请: 求你了 'please, I'm begging you'. It forms 要求 'demand', 请求 'request', 求助 'seek help' and 求婚 'to propose marriage'. It also means 'seek': 追求 'pursue'.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ qiú nǐ bié gàosu tā.
examples.english: I beg you not to tell him.

examples.hanzi: 他在找工作，想求别人帮忙。
examples.pinyin: Tā zài zhǎo gōngzuò, xiǎng qiú biérén bāngmáng.
examples.english: He's looking for a job and wants to ask others for help.

components.note: 刂 (knife) — cutting, as in 到, 分, 别: hard enough to cut.
冈 (gāng) gives the exact sound; also in 钢 gāng and 纲 gāng.

example.english: I just got home.
example.fact: 刚 sits before the verb: 刚来 'just arrived'. 刚才 'a moment ago' is a time word and can start a sentence. 刚好 means 'just right'. In writing 刚 also means 'firm': 刚强.

examples.pinyin: Tā gāng chūmén, nǐ zhǎo tā ma?
examples.english: He just stepped out, are you looking for him?

examples.pinyin: Zhè jiàn yīfu gānghǎo héshì.
examples.english: This dress fits just right.

components.note: 女 (woman) — women and family terms, as in 妈 mom, 好 good, 姐 sister; 女 (nǚ) also loosely echoes the rú sound.
口 (mouth) — speech; 如 originally meant "to follow, accord with", later "as, like"; also in 汝 rǔ and 茹 rú.
亻 (person) — people, as in 你, 他, 们; 何 was a person carrying a load (荷 hè).
可 (kě) is a close sound clue for hé; also in 河 hé, 歌 gē and 哥 gē.

example.hanzi: 我们应该如何解决这个问题?
example.pinyin: Wǒmen yīnggāi rúhé jiějué zhège wèntí?
example.english: How should we solve this problem?
example.fact: 如何 is the more formal, written-register cousin of 怎么样 — mentioned in this deck's pilot batch (rank 9) as the casual, spoken way to ask “how is X” — with 如何 dominating essays, news reports, and official questions, while 怎么样 rules everyday conversation.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ juéde zhè jiàn shì rúhé?
examples.english: What do you think about this?

examples.pinyin: Bùguǎn rúhé, wǒ dōu zhīchí nǐ.
examples.english: No matter what, I support you.

components.note: 比 (compare) — two people side by side, one lined up with the other; to compare.
贝 (cowrie) — money and value, as in 财, 货, 买: competing for prizes was once tied to offerings and stakes.

example.hanzi: 明天有一场重要的比赛。
example.pinyin: Míngtiān yǒu yì chǎng zhòngyào de bǐsài.
example.english: There's an important match tomorrow.
example.fact: 赛 relates to offering up valuables (built from 贝, shell-money), likely tied to ancient wager or prize customs, and 比 contributes “to compare” (two identical 匕 spoon-shapes side by side) — together 比赛 literally suggests “comparing while something valuable is at stake.”

examples.pinyin: Wǒmen duì yíngle zhè chǎng bǐsài.
examples.english: Our team won this match.

examples.pinyin: Tā cānjiāle yóuyǒng bǐsài.
examples.english: He took part in the swimming competition.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — marks speech and exclamations, as in 啊, 哎, 哦; 呀 is a soft particle.
牙 (yá) hints at the sound: 呀 ya is close to 芽 yá and 鸦 yā.

example.english: Come on, hurry up!
example.fact: 呀 is 啊 after a syllable ending in a, e, i, o or u: 好呀 'great!', 快来呀. In 哎呀 'oh dear' it is yā. It adds warmth or urgency.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ zěnme cái lái ya?
examples.english: Why have you only just arrived?

examples.pinyin: Zhēn piàoliang ya!
examples.english: How beautiful!

components.note: 忄 (heart) — feelings, as in 快 happy, 怕 afraid, 忙 busy.
青 (qīng) is a close sound clue for qíng; the series 清 qīng, 请 qǐng, 晴 qíng, 精 jīng.
兄 (xiōng) is only a loose sound clue for kuàng; the radical here is the ice form of 氵, as in 決.

example.pinyin: Qǐng gàosu wǒ xiànzài de qíngkuàng.
example.english: Please tell me the current situation.
example.fact: 况 also stands on its own as a formal adverb meaning 'moreover, furthermore' (何况, 况且) — a reminder that a character's contribution inside a compound word doesn't always match what it means as an independent word.

examples.pinyin: Nàr de qíngkuàng zěnmeyàng?
examples.english: What's the situation over there like?

examples.hanzi: 在这种情况下,我们只能等。
examples.pinyin: Zài zhè zhǒng qíngkuàng xià, wǒmen zhǐ néng děng.
examples.english: In this situation, we can only wait.

components.note: 又 (hand) — the bottom, standing in for the 攴 (tap) of traditional 變. 亦 on top replaces the tangled-thread part and has no meaning link.
變 (traditional) — tangled threads and a tapping hand 攴: sorting out a mess, so 'change'. Read as 'usually explained'.

example.english: The weather has turned cold.
example.fact: 变 + adjective + 了 means 'become': 变冷了, 变好了. It also makes nouns: 变化 'change', 变成 'turn into', 变得 + degree: 他变得很高 'he has become tall'.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ zuìjìn biànhuà zhēn dà.
examples.english: You've changed so much recently.

examples.pinyin: Hóngdēng biàn lǜdēng le.
examples.english: The red light turned green.

components.note: 关 (close) — simplified from 關, a gate 门 with a bolt across it; 关 also means "concern", as in 关系.
糸 (silk thread; 纟 on the left) — ties and connections, as in 红, 给, 经. 系 is a link or relation.

example.english: Their relationship is very good.
example.fact: 关系 covers far more ground than English 'relationship' — it's also the word behind "guānxi," the social capital and personal connections that grease business and favors in Chinese culture, so 有关系 can mean anything from 'related' to 'well-connected.'

examples.pinyin: Wǒ hé tā méiyǒu guānxi.
examples.english: I have no connection with him.

examples.pinyin: Méi guānxi, wǒ bú jièyì.
examples.english: It doesn't matter, I don't mind.

components.note: 真 (zhēn) is a sound clue for 镇 zhèn and 慎 shèn; 真 means real, true.
日 (sun) — on top; the usual explanation is sun over 正 "straight, correct": what is clear and straight is "right, is". A memory aid, not firm etymology.

example.pinyin: Zhēnshi, nǐ yòu wàng dài yàoshi le.
example.english: Honestly, you forgot your keys again.
example.fact: On its own, 真是 can stand as a complete interjection of mild exasperation ("真是!"), much like English "Honestly!" — a shift from its literal sense 'truly, indeed' that shows up constantly in casual complaints.

examples.pinyin: Zhēnshi de, yòu xiàyǔ le!
examples.english: Ugh, it's raining again!

examples.pinyin: Nǐ zhēn shì ge hǎorén.
examples.english: You're truly a good person.

components.note: 女 (woman) — a person kneeling with arms crossed; as a radical it heads many female and family words: 妈, 好, 姐.
士 (scholar, soldier) — usually read as an axe or weapon, so a warrior or gentleman (士兵, 博士). Memory aid: 士 has the longer bar on top, 土 (earth) on the bottom.

example.english: Welcome, ladies and gentlemen.
example.fact: 女士 is the neutral, marital-status-blind term for "Ms./madam" — unlike 小姐 (also in this batch), which traditionally named an unmarried young woman but has picked up a slang sense of "sex worker" in mainland China, making 女士 the safer default today.

examples.hanzi: 这位女士想点一杯咖啡。
examples.pinyin: Zhè wèi nǚshì xiǎng diǎn yì bēi kāfēi.
examples.english: This lady would like to order a coffee.

examples.pinyin: Nǚshìmen, xiānshengmen, wǎnshang hǎo!
examples.english: Ladies and gentlemen, good evening!

components.note: 木 (tree) — a tree with a mark at the base: the root, hence source, origin, and the measure word for books.

example.pinyin: Wǒ mǎi le yì běn shū.
example.english: I bought a book.
example.fact: 本 counts books and notebooks: 一本书. As 'root' it appears in 本来 'originally' and 根本 'fundamentally'. It also means 'this/our': 本人 'myself', 本月 'this month'. 日本 'Japan' means 'sun origin'.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ yǒu yì běn Zhōngwén cídiǎn.
examples.english: I have a Chinese dictionary.

examples.hanzi: 本来我想去，可是太累了。
examples.pinyin: Běnlái wǒ xiǎng qù, kěshì tài lèi le.
examples.english: I originally wanted to go, but I was too tired.

components.note: 马 (horse) — a galloping horse. As a radical it marks horses: 骑 ride, 驾 drive. It gives sound to 妈 mā, 吗 ma, 骂 mà and 码 mǎ.
上 (above) — a mark above a line, the mirror of 下 below.

example.english: I'll be right there.
example.fact: A popular, though linguistically disputed, folk etymology traces 马上 ('immediately') to imperial messengers who were already mounted and riding off — literally 'on the horse' (马 'horse' + 上 'on/above') — before finishing what they had to say.

examples.pinyin: Qǐng děng yíxià, wǒ mǎshàng huílái.
examples.english: Please wait, I'll be right back.

examples.hanzi: 听到消息,他马上打了电话。
examples.pinyin: Tīngdào xiāoxi, tā mǎshàng dǎle diànhuà.
examples.english: On hearing the news, he called right away.

components.note: 冫 (ice) — here the ice form of 氵 (water): 决 first meant to break a dam, so a decisive break.
夬 (guài) is a loose sound clue for jué; 夬 also sounds out 快 kuài and 块 kuài.
宀 (roof) — houses and shelter, as in 家 home, 安 safe, 客 guest; settling down under a roof.
正 (zhèng, upright; the lower part is written 疋) is a loose sound clue for dìng; also in 证 zhèng and 政 zhèng.

example.english: I've already decided.
example.fact: 决定 works as a verb ('to decide') and a noun ('a decision', as in 做决定) without changing form at all — the same zero-derivation trick behind other common verb-noun pairs like 工作 ('to work' / 'a job').

examples.pinyin: Nǐ juédìng qù nǎr le ma?
examples.english: Have you decided where to go?

examples.pinyin: Zhège juédìng hěn zhòngyào.
examples.english: This decision is very important.

components.note: 见 (see) — a big eye on a person's legs 儿: a person looking. The same 见 is in 现 appear, 觉 sense, 视 look.
至 (arrive) — 到 is to arrive.
刂 is the knife form 刀 (dāo), a close sound clue for dào; 到 itself sounds out 倒 dǎo/dào.

example.english: So glad to see you.
example.fact: 到 acts here as a resultative complement meaning 'successfully arrived at' — 见到 specifically marks that the seeing actually happened, the same pattern behind 找到 ('to find,' lit. 'seek-arrive') and 听到 ('to hear,' lit. 'listen-arrive').

examples.hanzi: 我在机场见到了老同学。
examples.pinyin: Wǒ zài jīchǎng jiàndàole lǎo tóngxué.
examples.english: I ran into an old classmate at the airport.

examples.pinyin: Hǎojiǔ bú jiàn, jiàndào nǐ zhēn hǎo!
examples.english: Long time no see, it's great to see you!

components.note: 木 (tree) — trees and wood, as in 树, 林, 本: 根 is a root.
艮 (gèn) is a close sound clue for gēn; 艮 also sounds out 跟 gēn and 很 hěn.
木 (tree) — a tree with a mark at the base: the root, hence source, origin, and the measure word for books.

example.english: This isn't a problem at all.
example.fact: 根本 starts life as a noun for 'root, foundation,' but slotted before 不 in a negative sentence it turns into an intensifier meaning 'not... at all' (根本不是) — an adverbial use that often surprises learners who first meet the word as a noun.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ gēnběn bú rènshi tā.
examples.english: I don't know him at all.

examples.pinyin: Zhège xiǎngfǎ gēnběn xíng bu tōng.
examples.english: This idea simply won't work.

components.note: 关 (close) — simplified from 關, a gate 门 with a bolt across it; 关 also means "concern", as in 关系.
于 (yú) is a sound clue for 宇 yǔ and 芋 yù; it is a light grammar word meaning "at, to".

example.hanzi: 这是一本关于历史的书。
example.pinyin: Zhè shì yì běn guānyú lìshǐ de shū.
example.english: This is a book about history.
example.fact: 关于 fronts the topic at the start of the phrase it introduces and can never be stranded at the end of a sentence the way English "about" can ("what's it about?") — the whole 关于-phrase has to come before what it describes.

examples.hanzi: 我想看关于旅行的电影。
examples.pinyin: Wǒ xiǎng kàn guānyú lǚxíng de diànyǐng.
examples.english: I want to watch a movie about travel.

examples.hanzi: 关于这件事,我们明天再谈。
examples.pinyin: Guānyú zhè jiàn shì, wǒmen míngtiān zài tán.
examples.english: About this matter, let's talk tomorrow.

components.note: 阝 on the right is 邑 (city) — places, as in 都 capital, 邮 post, 部 part. 那 was a place name before it meant "that".
儿 (child, legs) — shows a person's legs; in 兒 the top was a child's soft skull. As an ending (这儿) it adds the er sound; 儿 also in 先, 兄, 光.

example.english: The book is over there.
example.fact: 那儿 is the Beijing-flavored, r-suffixed twin of the more neutral 那里 — the same colloquial-vs-standard split already seen in 这里/这儿 for "here" — a register choice rather than a difference in meaning.

examples.pinyin: Tā zài nàr děng nǐ.
examples.english: He's waiting for you over there.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ cóng nàr guòlái de ma?
examples.english: Did you come from over there?

components.note: 隹 (zhuī, short-tailed bird) — 难 was first the name of a bird; "hard" is a borrowed use. The 又 here stands in for the traditional left part.

example.english: This question is very hard.
example.fact: 难 before a verb means 'hard to': 难吃 'bad-tasting', 难看 'ugly', 难过 'sad'. Read nàn it means 'disaster': 灾难 'calamity'. Its opposite is 容易 or 简单.

examples.pinyin: Xué Zhōngwén bú tài nán.
examples.english: Learning Chinese isn't too hard.

examples.pinyin: Zhè dào tí hěn nán huídá.
examples.english: This question is hard to answer.

components.note: 只 (only; measure word) — two old characters merged: 隻 zhī "a single (bird), measure word" and 只 zhǐ "only".
要 (want, need) — oldest form shows hands at a waist: it meant "waist" (腰 yāo adds 月 flesh); "essential" followed.

example.pinyin: Zhǐyào nǐ nǔlì, jiù néng chénggōng.
example.english: As long as you work hard, you can succeed.
example.fact: 只要 almost never appears alone — it sets up a sufficient condition completed later in the sentence by 就 ("then"), forming the paired frame 只要...,就..., a structural cousin of 因为...所以... and 虽然...但是....

examples.hanzi: 只要有时间,我就去看你。
examples.pinyin: Zhǐyào yǒu shíjiān, wǒ jiù qù kàn nǐ.
examples.english: As long as I have time, I'll come see you.

examples.hanzi: 只要多练习,你一定能说好。
examples.pinyin: Zhǐyào duō liànxí, nǐ yídìng néng shuō hǎo.
examples.english: As long as you practice more, you'll surely speak well.

meanings: variant of 裡面|里面[li3 mian4]

components.note: 田 (field) — farmland, the village's fields.
土 (earth) — land; field + earth gives "village" and then the unit of distance. 里 is the sound part of 理 lǐ.
面 (face) — a picture of a face; extended to the surface or side of things, as in 外面 outside.

example.english: What's inside the box?
example.fact: 里面 follows the noun it locates rather than preceding it ("箱子里面," literally "box inside") — like 上面 and 外面, it behaves more like a postposition than the preposition English "inside" is.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ de shǒujī zài bāo lǐmiàn.
examples.english: My phone is inside the bag.

examples.hanzi: 里面太热了,我们出去吧。
examples.pinyin: Lǐmiàn tài rè le, wǒmen chūqù ba.
examples.english: It's too hot inside, let's go out.

components.note: 母 (mǔ) is a close sound clue for měi; the same part also in 海 hǎi, 梅 méi and 悔 huǐ.

example.english: I run every morning.
example.fact: 每 goes before a measure word or time: 每个人 'everyone', 每天 'every day', 每次 'each time'. 每个人 is usually followed by 都: 每个人都知道.

examples.hanzi: 每个人都有自己的想法。
examples.pinyin: Měi ge rén dōu yǒu zìjǐ de xiǎngfǎ.
examples.english: Everyone has their own ideas.

examples.hanzi: 我每个周末都去看奶奶。
examples.pinyin: Wǒ měi ge zhōumò dōu qù kàn nǎinai.
examples.english: I visit grandma every weekend.

components.note: 亻 (person radical, 单人旁) — people and what they do: 你, 他, 位; 份 is a person's portion or share.
分 (fēn) is a near sound match for fèn; also 粉 fěn and 纷 fēn.

example.english: I'd like one portion of fried rice.
example.fact: 份 counts portions of food (一份饭), jobs (一份工作), newspapers (一份报纸) and documents. 身份 means 'identity', 月份 'month'.

examples.pinyin: Qǐng gěi wǒ yí fèn càidān.
examples.english: Please give me a menu.

examples.pinyin: Tā zhǎodàole yí fèn xīn gōngzuò.
examples.english: He found a new job.

meanings: when all is said and done

components.note: 至 (arrive) — 到 is to arrive.
刂 is the knife form 刀 (dāo), a close sound clue for dào; 到 itself sounds out 倒 dǎo/dào.
广 (shelter) — buildings, as in 店 shop, 床 bed, 度 degree; 底 is the base of a house.
氐 (dī) is a close sound clue for dǐ; also in 低 dī and 抵 dǐ.

example.english: What exactly are you trying to say?
example.fact: 到底 shows up constantly in impatient or emphatic questions ("到底是谁?" "Who exactly is it?") — its literal image, "to the bottom," matches the English idiom "get to the bottom of it" almost exactly.

examples.pinyin: Nǐ dàodǐ qù bu qù?
examples.english: Are you going or not, after all?

examples.pinyin: Tā dàodǐ háishi lái le.
examples.english: He came in the end after all.

components.note: 子 (child) — 了 is usually read as a swaddled baby, like 子 without the arms. Its meanings 'finish' (了解 liǎo) and the particle le were borrowed later.
角 (horn) — an ox's horn; with 刀 (knife) the picture is cutting up an ox, so "to take apart", then to loosen and explain.
刀 (knife) — cutting, as in 分, 切, 到; a blade separates the parts.

example.english: I want to understand you better.
example.fact: 了 is read liǎo here, not the far more common particle reading le — one of a handful of high-frequency characters (also 还 hái/huán, 觉 jué/jiào) whose pronunciation depends entirely on which word it is part of.

examples.pinyin: Wǒ bú tài liǎojiě zhège chéngshì.
examples.english: I don't know this city very well.

examples.pinyin: Tā hěn liǎojiě wǒ de xiǎngfǎ.
examples.english: He understands my thinking well.
